newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Seoul at new low, profit-takers hit Asian markets.
newsitem.headline: Seoul at new low, profit-takers hit Asian markets.

text.p: Seoul stocks continued their slide, falling to a new 33-month low on Tuesday due to continuing fears over the economy and aftershocks from Monday's sentencing of nine business tycoons.
Trade was generally quiet throughout Asia, with dull markets in Tokyo and Singapore finishing slightly higher and Seoul, Hong Kong and Jakarta declining on profit-taking.
Seoul's composite stock index fell 5.14 points, or 0.67 percent, to provisionally close at 761.75. It was the lowest since November 3, 1993, when the index dropped to 756.87.
"The market looked like it was recovering in the morning, but then profit-taking emerged in smaller shares which had fared well recently," said Choi Chul-oong of Sunkyong Securities.

Choi said poor sentiment was further soured by the central bank's announcement of lower-than-expected gross domestic product (GDP) growth figures. GDP grew by a real 6.7 percent in the second quarter against a 9.7 percent rise a year earlier.
Shares of Daewoo Corp, Dong-Ah Construction, Hanbo Steel, and Jinro group dropped, a day after a South Korean court sentenced their chairmen to prison on bribery charges.

Tokyo stocks closed marginally higher after a rebound in the morning had withered. Turnover was the lightest this year, with institutional investors waiting for the Bank of Japan's (BOJ) key "tankan" survey due out on Wednesday, brokers said.
The key Nikkei 225 average finished up 26.53 points or 0.13 percent at 20,910.27, after briefly bouncing back to 21,022.41.
In Hong Kong, renewed fears of rising interest rates pushed stocks down, with investors prompted to take profits after recent gains following a rise in the U.S. long bond yield.
The Hang Seng closed 85.71 points or 0.75 percent lower at 11,338.93. The market was closed on Monday for Liberation Day.
Jakarta share prices closed lower in slow trading following local profit-taking in selected second-liners and big-caps, brokers said.
The Jakarta Composite Index fell 3.22 points, or 0.58 percent, to close at 549.52 points.
Singapore's key share index finished marginally higher in quiet trading with two rumoured takeover target stocks dominating volume and gains.
Brokers said that but for the two stocks -- Transmarco and Metro Holdings -- the volume would have been still thinner.
The key Straits Times Industrials Index finished up 11.42 points, or 0.53 percent, at 2,171.45.

Investor disinterest in Malaysia kept larger counters in the doldrums, with the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange Composite Index easing 2.92 points, or 0.26 percent, to 1,113.45. Blue chips continued to flounder in spite of a positive trade report.

But Malaysian Second Board stocks surged 3.10 percent to a new closing high, helped by a continued dose of retail-led buying. The Second Board index jumped 16.13 points to 537.12, eclipsing its previous high of 520.99 set on Monday.
The Australian sharemarket closed lower, with losses steepening in the afternoon session as nervous investors trimmed positions ahead of market action in the U.S. later today.
The All Ordinaries index closed down 19.8 points, or 0.87 percent, at 2,262.3.

The dollar, bruised by fairly strong overseas sales in thin trade, had dipped across the board by late Tokyo trade, although it had rebounded from earlier lows against the yen. At 1152 GMT, the dollar traded at 107.74/79 yen and 1.4746/56 marks.
Brent October futures prices were traded lower compared with London's settlement on Friday, but narrowed the arbitrage against NYMEX.
October Brent last traded at $20.14 per barrel, down 27 cents from Brent's settlement on Friday in London. SIMEX and London Brent markets were closed on Monday to mark a national holiday in the U.K.
Hong Kong bullion ended slightly lower at US$388.90/389.40 an ounce against New York's US$389.20/70 close on Monday.
